etymology: From the Saxon rihtwis, right-wise — wise in the right, ordered to the rule. The Hebrew tsaddiq comes from a root of straightness and correct measure, and the Greek dikaios from dike, the settled rule of judgment. The English word therefore carries what both originals carry: conformity to a standard outside the man.
biblical_def: Righteous describes a man as he stands measured against the law of God, not as he stands measured against his neighbours or against himself. Scripture uses the word two ways that must be held together. Absolutely, no son of Adam is righteous: “As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10). Yet God calls particular men righteous and does so truly — “thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation” (Genesis 7:1) — and the difference between those two statements is the whole gospel. Noah is not righteous by an obedience that survived the ruin of the fall; he is righteous by a righteousness reckoned to him, the same righteousness Abraham received when he believed God. The Reformed doctrine of justification is simply this word handled honestly: the believer is declared righteous on the ground of Christ's active and passive obedience imputed to him, not on the ground of any goodness found in him. What follows from the declaration is real: the man so declared begins to live the part. The LORD marks out his way and keeps it — “For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish” (Psalm 1:6) — and his prayers carry weight, for “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (James 5:16). The declaration comes first and the walk follows; reverse them and the gospel is lost.
webster_summary: Just, upright, conformed to the divine law. In Scripture no man is righteous in himself; the believer is declared righteous by a righteousness imputed to him, and then walks accordingly.
webster_full: RIGHTEOUS, a. richyus. [Sax. rihtwis; riht, right, and wis, wise.] Just; accordant to the divine law.
2. Just; equitable; merited; as, a righteous doom or sentence.
3. Applied to God, holy in all his ways, and just in all his dealings with men.
4. In Scripture, one who is justified — not innocent in himself, but accounted righteous through faith.
5. The righteous, in the plural, denotes the people of God collectively; as, the way of the righteous, Psa. 1.
corruption_summary: The modern ear hears righteous and thinks self-righteous — a posture, a scowl, a claim to be better than others. Scripture's word means the opposite: a standing given to men who confessedly have none of their own.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has been hollowed out from two directions at once. From the world, righteous has become a synonym for priggish, so that to be called righteous is now an accusation; the only remaining respectable use is the ironic one. From within the church, a moralism that Paul spent Romans and Galatians demolishing keeps reasserting itself, and men set about being righteous in order to be accepted rather than living righteously because they have been accepted. Both errors miss the same point. Romans 3:10 leaves nobody standing, and it is quoted from the Psalms precisely so that the man most confident of his record will find himself named in it.

The recovery is the doctrine of imputation. Christ's obedience — active in his perfect keeping of the law, passive in his bearing of its curse — is reckoned to the believer's account, and the believer's sin was reckoned to his. That is why Genesis can call Noah righteous without contradicting Romans: the verdict rests on a righteousness received, not achieved. A man who understands this cannot be self-righteous, because he knows exactly where the righteousness came from, and he cannot be careless either, because the God who declared him righteous also knows his way and intends to keep it.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaddiq is the just man measured by a straight rule; the verb tsadaq in the causative stem means to declare just, which is the forensic sense the Reformers recovered. Greek dikaios and the verb dikaioo carry the same courtroom force.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaddiq (H6662) — just, lawful, righteous; the man who answers to the standard.
Hebrew tsadaq (H6663) — to be just; in the causative stem, to declare or pronounce just, as a judge does.
Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666) — righteousness; that which Abraham had counted to him for believing.
Greek dikaios (G1342) — righteous, just, conformed to dike, the rule of right.
Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to justify, to declare righteous; a verdict pronounced, never a quality infused.
usage: Of the universal verdict on fallen men: there is none righteous, no, not one (Romans 3:10).
Of a particular man God himself names righteous: thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation (Genesis 7:1).
Of the prayers such a man offers: the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much (James 5:16).
scriptures: Romans 3:10
As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one:
Genesis 7:1
And the LORD said unto Noah, Come thou and all thy house into the ark; for thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation.
Psalm 1:6
For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish.
James 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.

etymology: From the Saxon mihtig, from miht, might. Hebrew gibbor is the warrior-strong man, from gabar, to prevail; the same root gives the divine title El Gibbor, the mighty God.
biblical_def: Mighty in Scripture is a word about ability to accomplish, and it is applied to men and to God in a deliberately unequal way. Of men it is often a warning. Nimrod is the first man the Bible calls mighty — “He was a mighty hunter before the LORD” (Genesis 10:9) — and the phrase before the LORD is not praise but exposure; the builder of Babel's kingdom is mighty in the sight of the God he defies. Of God the word is a title. Isaiah names the child born to us The mighty God (Isaiah 9:6), setting the whole weight of divine omnipotence on an infant, and Zephaniah puts the same might in the middle of his people: “The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save” (Zephaniah 3:17). Mary's song holds the two senses together and shows how God uses his might — “For he that is mighty hath done to me great things” (Luke 1:49) — the Almighty stooping to a village girl of no account. That is the pattern throughout: divine might is not raw force but power directed by covenant love, and it characteristically overturns the might of men. God chooses the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
webster_summary: Having great power or strength. In Scripture a title of God (The mighty God) and a frequent caution against men, whose might God delights to overturn by the weak.
webster_full: MIGHTY, a. [Sax. mihtig, from miht, might.] Having great bodily strength or physical power; very strong; as, a mighty man of valor.
2. Very great in ability, or in the power of doing; as, mighty in the scriptures.
3. Very great in extent or effect; as, a mighty work; a mighty deliverance.
4. Applied to God, omnipotent; as, the mighty God, Isa. 9.
5. As a noun, the mighty denotes men of power and rank; as, God chose the weak to confound the mighty, 1 Cor. 1.
corruption_summary: Might in modern usage is measured by output — reach, budget, influence — and God's might is then imagined as the same thing enlarged. Scripture measures might by what it accomplishes for a covenant people, and shows it stooping.
corruption_paragraphs: Two mistakes attend this word. The first treats divine omnipotence as bare capacity, a store of force detached from character, which produces the old sophistry about whether God can make a stone too heavy to lift. Scripture never presents might that way. The mighty God of Isaiah 9:6 is named alongside Wonderful, Counsellor, everlasting Father, Prince of Peace — his power is inseparable from his wisdom, his fatherhood, and his peace, because God is simple and not a bundle of separable attributes.

The second mistake is nearer home: the assumption that God works through the mighty. Every revival strategy built on securing the influential, and every congregation that quietly esteems its wealthy members, rests on it. Paul says the opposite in flat terms, and Mary sang it before him — he that is mighty regarded the low estate of his handmaiden. The principle to recover is that God's might is displayed most plainly where human might is absent, and a church that forgets this will spend its strength courting the very people God passes by.
roots_summary: Hebrew gibbor, the prevailing warrior, from gabar, to be strong; El Gibbor is the divine title. Greek dunatos is the able one, from dunamis, power, and krataios stresses gripping strength.
roots_lines: Hebrew gibbor (H1368) — mighty man, warrior; used of Nimrod, of David's men, and of God himself.
Hebrew gabar (H1396) — to prevail, to be strong; the root behind both the warrior and the title.
Hebrew El Gibbor — the mighty God; the title Isaiah 9:6 lays upon the child born to us.
Greek dunatos (G1415) — powerful, able; the adjective behind the things which are mighty.
Greek dunamis (G1411) — power, might; the noun Paul uses of the gospel and of the Spirit.
usage: Of a man mighty in the sight of the God he defied: he was a mighty hunter before the LORD (Genesis 10:9).
Of the Son as a divine title: his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God (Isaiah 9:6).
Of God's might exercised toward the lowly: he that is mighty hath done to me great things (Luke 1:49).
scriptures: Genesis 10:9
He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.
Isaiah 9:6

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
Zephaniah 3:17
The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.
Luke 1:49
For he that is mighty hath done to me great things; and holy is his name.

pos: a. (complete, whole, entire; rendering Hebrew tamim, Greek teleios)
etymology: From the Latin perfectus, perficio, to finish through — carried to its end. Hebrew tamim means whole, sound, without blemish, and is the word for an unblemished sacrificial animal; Greek teleios is from telos, an end or goal, and means having reached its intended completion.
biblical_def: Perfect in the Authorized Version rarely means sinless. It means whole, complete, entire, brought to the end for which the thing was made. Job is called “perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil” (Job 1:1), and the book then spends forty chapters showing a man who is manifestly not sinless; tamim describes his integrity, the absence of a divided heart, not the absence of sin. The same word governs the sacrificial law, where a perfect lamb is an unblemished one — sound, entire, fit to be offered. Of things that come from God the word can be taken absolutely: “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psalm 19:7), lacking nothing it should contain. Of men it is a word of direction as much as of state. When our Lord says “Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect” (Matthew 5:48), the context is loving enemies, and the sense is completeness of love that does not stop at the boundary of those who love us in return — a whole love answering to a whole God. The covenant charge to Abram sets the same direction: “I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect” (Genesis 17:1), where wholeness of walk is commanded on the ground of who God is. Perfection is thus the goal toward which sanctification genuinely moves, reached not in this life but at glorification.
webster_summary: Complete, whole, entire, without blemish — not, in most biblical usage, sinless. Job is perfect in integrity; a lamb is perfect in soundness; the law is perfect absolutely.
webster_full: PERFECT, a. [L. perfectus, perficio, to complete; per and facio, to do.] Finished; complete; consummate; not defective; having all that is requisite to its nature and kind.
2. Fully informed; completely skilled; as, perfect in the art.
3. Complete in moral excellencies; blameless; as, a perfect heart.
4. In Scripture, upright and sincere, without a divided heart; as, Job was perfect and upright, Job 1.
5. Of a sacrifice, sound and without blemish; as, your lamb shall be perfect, Exod. 12.
corruption_summary: Read as sinless, the word breeds either perfectionism or despair. Read as Scripture uses it — whole, undivided, unblemished — it describes an integrity God actually works in his people now.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors grow from the same mistranslation. Wesleyan and later holiness teaching read perfect as attainable sinlessness in this life and produced a doctrine of entire sanctification that Scripture will not carry; the same Job who is called perfect abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes. Running the other way, an honest man who reads Matthew 5:48 as a demand for sinlessness concludes the command is impossible and quietly files it away. Both readings mistake wholeness for flawlessness.

There is also a flattening in modern speech, where perfect has become a courtesy noise — an answer to a confirmed appointment. A word emptied by overuse cannot bear the weight of Psalm 19:7. The principle to recover is the sacrificial sense that underlies the whole vocabulary: what is offered to God must be entire, unblemished, not the leftover or the divided. That standard condemns half-hearted worship far more searchingly than a demand for sinlessness would, and it points where the whole system points, to the one unblemished Lamb whose perfection is reckoned to those who trust him.
roots_summary: Hebrew tamim is whole and unblemished, from tamam, to be complete; it is the sacrificial standard. Greek teleios is from telos, the end or goal, and denotes a thing that has arrived at what it was for.
roots_lines: Hebrew tamim (H8549) — whole, sound, without blemish; the required quality of a sacrifice.
Hebrew tamam (H8552) — to be complete, to be finished; the verbal root behind the adjective.
Hebrew tom (H8537) — integrity, simplicity of heart; the undivided quality ascribed to Job.
Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, full-grown, having reached its telos.
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend or fit together; the verb behind make you perfect in Hebrews 13:21.
usage: Of a man's undivided integrity, not his sinlessness: that man was perfect and upright (Job 1:1).
Of the law taken absolutely: the law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul (Psalm 19:7).
Of wholeness of walk commanded on the ground of who God is: walk before me, and be thou perfect (Genesis 17:1).
scriptures: Job 1:1
There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil.
Psalm 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
Matthew 5:48
Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.
Genesis 17:1
And when Abram was ninety years old and nine, the LORD appeared to Abram, and said unto him, I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect.

pos: a. (having wisdom, skilled in right living; rendering Hebrew chakam, Greek sophos)
etymology: From the Saxon wis, knowing, from the root of wit, to know. Hebrew chakam is first a word of practical skill — the craftsman of the tabernacle is chakam-hearted — and only then of moral discernment; the Hebrew never separates knowing from doing.
biblical_def: Wise in Scripture describes skill in living rightly before God, and it begins not with intelligence but with fear. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; a man may be learned and not wise, and Scripture repeatedly says so. The word's Hebrew background is the workshop: the men who built the tabernacle were wise-hearted, meaning skilled, and biblical wisdom keeps that flavour of competence applied to the actual business of living. A wise man is therefore teachable before he is anything else — “A wise man will hear, and will increase learning” (Proverbs 1:5) — and the fool by contrast is the man who has stopped listening. Scripture also insists that wisdom is granted, not merely acquired: the testimony of the LORD is sure, “making wise the simple” (Psalm 19:7), and the holy scriptures “are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15). That last phrase sets the boundary of the word's worth: wisdom that does not run to Christ is not finally wisdom at all. Our Lord commends a shrewdness that is never cynical — “be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Matthew 10:16) — discernment about men held together with innocence toward them.
webster_summary: Skilled in right living, discerning, taught of God. Biblical wisdom begins in the fear of the LORD, is granted through the Scriptures, and is aimed finally at salvation in Christ.
webster_full: WISE, a. s as z. [Sax. wis; G. weise.] Properly, having knowledge; hence, having the power of discerning and judging correctly what is right, and of selecting the best means to accomplish it.
2. Discreet and judicious in the use of means; prudent; as, wise as serpents, Matt. 10.
3. Skilful; dexterous; as, the wise-hearted workmen of the tabernacle, Exod. 36.
4. In Scripture, godly; pious; instructed in the way of salvation; as, wise unto salvation, 2 Tim. 3.
5. Sometimes ironically, worldly-wise; as, the wisdom of this world, which God will confound, 1 Cor. 1.
corruption_summary: Wisdom has been reduced to information on one side and to sentiment on the other — either data or a warm feeling about the universe. Scripture makes it skill in living, rooted in the fear of God and ending in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The academic reduction treats wisdom as accumulated knowledge, which is why an age with unprecedented access to information is so plainly short of wisdom. Scripture separates the two flatly: the wise man is the one who hears and increases learning, meaning he remains correctable, while the fool may know a great deal and be unteachable. The therapeutic reduction runs the other way, making wisdom a matter of inner attunement, listening to oneself, trusting one's instincts — the exact counsel Proverbs spends thirty-one chapters contradicting, since the heart is deceitful above all things.

Both reductions drop the fear of the LORD, which is where the Bible says wisdom starts, and both drop the destination, which is Christ. Paul says God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and that judgment falls on the credentialed and the intuitive alike. The recovery is 2 Timothy 3:15: the Scriptures make a man wise unto salvation, and any wisdom that leaves him unsaved has failed at the only point that finally matters.
roots_summary: Hebrew chakam is skilled, from a root of craftsmanship applied to conduct; chokmah is the wisdom personified in Proverbs 8. Greek sophos is the wise man and phronimos the prudent, the word behind wise as serpents.
roots_lines: Hebrew chakam (H2450) — wise, skilful; used of the tabernacle craftsmen and of the godly man alike.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; personified in Proverbs 8 and fulfilled in Christ.
Hebrew yirath YHWH — the fear of the LORD, named in Proverbs 9:10 as the beginning of wisdom.
Greek sophos (G4680) — wise; used both of God's wisdom and, ironically, of the world's.
Greek phronimos (G5429) — prudent, shrewd; the word in be ye therefore wise as serpents.
usage: Of teachableness as the mark of wisdom: a wise man will hear, and will increase learning (Proverbs 1:5).
Of shrewdness joined to innocence: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves (Matthew 10:16).
Of the Scriptures' saving purpose: able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 3:15).
scriptures: Proverbs 1:5
A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels:
Matthew 10:16
Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
2 Timothy 3:15
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Psalm 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.

pos: a. (having strength, firm, secure; rendering Hebrew chazaq, Greek ischuros)
etymology: From the Saxon strang, strong. Hebrew chazaq means to bind fast, to seize and hold, and so to be firm; the imperative chazaq given to Joshua is less feel strong than take hold, hold fast.
biblical_def: Strong in Scripture is almost always a command before it is a description, and the command is never addressed to a man's reserves. Joshua is told “Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest” (Joshua 1:9), and the for carries the whole weight: the strength commanded rests on a presence promised, not on a temperament possessed. Paul repeats the structure exactly — “be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might” (Ephesians 6:10) — and then arms the man with a panoply that is all God's own. The Old Testament gives the image its home: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Proverbs 18:10). Strength here is a place a man runs to, not a quality he generates; the running is his, the tower is not. Paul's charge to the Corinthians gathers the whole into four short imperatives — “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1 Corinthians 16:13) — where being strong is set beside standing fast in the faith, so that the strength in view is doctrinal steadiness under pressure as much as courage in action.
webster_summary: Firm, able to endure, secure. Every biblical command to be strong is grounded on God's presence or power, never on the man's own reserves; the strong tower is a place to run to.
webster_full: STRONG, a. [Sax. strang.] Having physical active power, or great power of acting; as, a strong man.
2. Having power to resist attacks; firm; secure; as, a strong fortress or tower.
3. Firm in opinion or purpose; steadfast; as, strong in the faith.
4. Powerful in operation or effect; as, strong drink; a strong argument.
5. In Scripture, be strong in the Lord, that is, made firm by his power, Eph. 6.
corruption_summary: Strength is now spoken of as an inner resource to be located and drawn upon — find your strength, be your own strength. Scripture commands strength and then points away from the man to the tower he must run into.
corruption_paragraphs: The self-sourced account of strength is everywhere, and it is cruel to the people who need strength most, because it sends a man looking inside for what is not there. Scripture is more honest about human weakness and more generous about its remedy. Joshua is not told to summon resolve; he is told God will be with him wherever he goes, and to act accordingly. Paul does not tell the Ephesians to be strong; he tells them to be strong in the Lord, and every piece of armour he then names belongs to God before it belongs to them.

There is a churchly version of the same error, in which strength becomes a personality type and the quiet, the ill, and the grieving are made to feel sub-Christian. Proverbs 18:10 corrects it: the righteous runneth into the tower. Running to safety is not what the world calls strength, yet it is precisely the act Scripture commends, and a man too proud to run is not strong but exposed. The principle to recover is that biblical strength is derivative — borrowed, garrisoned, held fast by another — and that this is not a lesser strength but the only kind that holds.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazaq is to seize and hold fast, hence to be firm; oz is strength as a refuge, the word behind strong tower. Greek ischuros is the mighty one and endunamoo the verb be strengthened within.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to bind fast, to hold, to be strong; the imperative given to Joshua.
Hebrew oz (H5797) — strength, might, refuge; God is called the strength of his people.
Hebrew migdal oz — strong tower; the figure of Proverbs 18:10 for the name of the LORD.
Greek ischuros (G2478) — strong, mighty, forcible; used of God and of the strong man armed.
Greek endunamoo (G1743) — to empower, to strengthen inwardly; Paul's verb in Ephesians 6:10.
usage: Of strength commanded on the ground of God's presence: be strong and of a good courage… for the LORD thy God is with thee (Joshua 1:9).
Of the name of God as a refuge: the name of the LORD is a strong tower (Proverbs 18:10).
Of doctrinal steadiness under pressure: stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong (1 Corinthians 16:13).
scriptures: Joshua 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
Ephesians 6:10
Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.
Proverbs 18:10
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
1 Corinthians 16:13
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.

pos: a. (entire, complete; also sound, healed; rendering Hebrew kol, Greek holos and hugies)
etymology: From the Saxon hal, sound, well — the same root that gives hale, heal, and holy. English preserves in one word what Scripture holds together: to be whole is to be unbroken, and to be healed is to be made whole again.
biblical_def: Whole carries two senses in the Authorized Version that turn out to be one. It means entire, the sum and not a part: “Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13). And it means sound, unbroken, restored — the word for healing. Our Lord uses the second sense with deliberate irony: “They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick” (Matthew 9:12), spoken to men who were not whole and did not know it. To the woman with the issue of blood he says, “Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague” (Mark 5:34) — and the word covers both her body and her standing, for she had been cut off by the law of uncleanness and is now sent away in peace. Paul gathers the senses into a prayer for the whole man: “I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Scripture knows nothing of a soul saved out of a body discarded; the redemption in view is of the entire man, and it is completed at the resurrection.
webster_summary: Entire, complete, all of a thing; and also sound or healed. The English word carries both senses because Scripture does — the healed man is the man made whole again.
webster_full: WHOLE, a. hole. [Sax. hal, sound, whole; the root of heal and hale.] All; total; containing the total amount or number; as, the whole earth; the whole matter.
2. Complete; entire; not defective or imperfect; as, a whole duty.
3. Sound; not broken; as, a whole vessel.
4. Restored to health; healed; as, thy faith hath made thee whole, Mark 5.
5. In Scripture, the whole man, spirit and soul and body, 1 Thess. 5.
corruption_summary: Wholeness has been taken over as a therapeutic goal — self-integration, feeling entire. Scripture's wholeness is made, not achieved, and it comes to those who first admit they are not whole.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern vocabulary of wholeness locates the problem in fragmentation and the cure in integration: a man is to gather up his parts and become entire by his own inner work. Scripture agrees that man is broken and disagrees entirely about the remedy. The woman in Mark 5 did not integrate herself; she touched Christ's garment and was made whole, and the passive voice is the doctrine. Matthew 9:12 exposes the harder problem — the men who most needed the physician were the ones convinced they were already whole, and self-assessment is precisely the faculty sin has damaged.

The recovery runs through 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Biblical wholeness is not psychological unity but the preservation of the entire man — spirit and soul and body — blameless unto the coming of Christ, which means it is eschatological and God does it. That has two consequences worth holding. It forbids the false spirituality that treats the body as incidental to salvation, since the body is named in the prayer. And it relieves the believer of an impossible project, because the God of peace who sanctifies is the one who will also perform it: faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it.
roots_summary: Hebrew kol is all or the whole; shalem is whole in the sense of complete and at peace, cognate with shalom. Greek holos is entire and hugies is sound or healthy, the word behind made whole.
roots_lines: Hebrew kol (H3605) — all, the whole, every; the ordinary word for totality.
Hebrew shalem (H8003) — whole, complete, at peace; kin to shalom, which is wholeness rather than mere quiet.
Greek holos (G3650) — whole, entire; behind your whole spirit and soul and body.
Greek hugies (G5199) — sound, healthy, whole; the word for a healed man, giving English hygiene.
Greek sozo (G4982) — to save, to make whole; the same verb serves for healing the body and saving the soul.
usage: Of the sum of a man's obligation: fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man (Ecclesiastes 12:13).
Of those who think they need no physician: they that be whole need not a physician (Matthew 9:12).
Of the entire man preserved to the last day: your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless (1 Thessalonians 5:23).
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 12:13
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
Matthew 9:12
But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
Mark 5:34
And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague.
1 Thessalonians 5:23
And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

pos: a. (having power or capacity; rendering Hebrew yakol, Greek dunatos)
etymology: From the Latin habilis, apt, fit, from habeo, to have or hold. Hebrew yakol means to be able, to prevail, to endure; Greek dunatos is from dunamai, to be capable, and is the root of English dynamic.
biblical_def: Able is a small word that carries some of the largest confessions in Scripture, because it is the word faith uses about God when circumstances are against it. The three Hebrews standing before the furnace state it precisely: “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king” (Daniel 3:17) — and their next words, but if not, show that ability confessed is not deliverance presumed. Paul uses the word for the reach of God's power beyond the limits of prayer and imagination: God is “able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think” (Ephesians 3:20). He uses it again in prison as the ground of his own settled confidence — “I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day” (2 Timothy 1:12) — where the object of trust is a Person, not a proposition. Jude closes with the same word turned toward perseverance: God is “able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy” (Jude 1:24). Taken together these say that the believer's security rests on divine ability, not human grip.
webster_summary: Having sufficient power or capacity. In Scripture the characteristic word of faith about God — able to deliver, able to do above all we ask, able to keep from falling.
webster_full: ABLE, a. [L. habilis, from habeo, to have or hold.] Having physical power sufficient; having competent power or strength, bodily or mental.
2. Having strong or unusual powers of mind; as, an able minister.
3. Having competent means or resources; as, able to bear the charge.
4. Having the requisite legal qualifications; as, able to inherit.
5. In Scripture, applied chiefly to God; as, God is able to make all grace abound, 2 Cor. 9.
corruption_summary: Able is now heard mainly in the vocabulary of human capacity and its measurement. Scripture's dominant use is the opposite — a confession of God's power made precisely where human capacity has run out.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word's ordinary sense is stable; what has thinned is the habit of using it about God. Where an older piety said he is able, a functionally deist Christianity says we will do what we can, and prayer contracts to the size of what is already plausible. Ephesians 3:20 was written against exactly that contraction: God is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, so the ceiling is neither our request nor our imagination.

The principle to recover is the balance Daniel 3 strikes and modern usage loses in both directions. The three Hebrews neither doubted the ability nor presumed the outcome: our God is able to deliver, and he will deliver us out of thine hand — but if not, we still will not serve thy gods. Confessing God's ability is not a technique for securing a result, which is where prosperity teaching goes wrong, and declining to presume the result is not unbelief, which is where its critics sometimes overcorrect. Faith says able and then leaves the outcome with the one who is.
roots_summary: Hebrew yakol is to be able, to prevail, to endure. Greek dunamai is to be capable and dunatos the adjective; the compound hikanos adds the sense of sufficiency, being enough for the thing required.
roots_lines: Hebrew yakol (H3201) — to be able, to prevail; used of God's power and of man's limits.
Greek dunamai (G1410) — to be able, to have power; the verb behind the confession God is able.
Greek dunatos (G1415) — able, powerful; the adjective used of God in Romans 4:21.
Greek hikanos (G2425) — sufficient, competent, enough; Paul's word for ministerial sufficiency in 2 Corinthians 3:5.
Greek phulasso (G5442) — to guard, to keep; the verb Jude joins to able in able to keep you from falling.
usage: Of faith confessing power without presuming outcome: our God whom we serve is able to deliver us (Daniel 3:17).
Of God's reach beyond prayer and imagination: able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20).
Of the ground of perseverance: able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless (Jude 1:24).
scriptures: Daniel 3:17
If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.
Ephesians 3:20
Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us,
2 Timothy 1:12

For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.
Jude 1:24
Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy,

pos: a. (full of grace, favourable, kind; rendering Hebrew channun, Greek chrestos)
etymology: From the Latin gratiosus, from gratia, favour. Hebrew channun comes from chanan, to stoop in kindness to an inferior — the picture is of a superior bending down, which is why the adjective is used of God far more often than of men.
biblical_def: Gracious describes God as he inclines toward those who have no claim on him. The word belongs to the formula that runs through the Old Testament like a refrain: “The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy” (Psalm 103:8), and again “The LORD is gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy” (Psalm 145:8). This is God's own self-disclosure, first given to Moses at the rock and then quoted back to him by his people for a thousand years. Its most striking appearance is on the lips of a man who resented it. Jonah, furious that Nineveh was spared, explains that this is exactly why he fled: “I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil” (Jonah 4:2). The graciousness of God is not a discovery that pleases everyone; a man who wants his enemies destroyed finds it intolerable. Peter turns the word into the ground of Christian appetite — “If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious” (1 Peter 2:3) — where grace is something known by tasting, not merely granted as a doctrine, and the tasting is what makes a believer desire the sincere milk of the word.
webster_summary: Disposed to show unmerited favour; kind to those with no claim. The great Old Testament refrain — merciful and gracious, slow to anger — is God's own description of himself.
webster_full: GRACIOUS, a. [L. gratiosus, from gratia, favor.] Favorable; kind; benevolent; disposed to forgive offenses and impart unmerited blessings.
2. Proceeding from divine grace; as, a gracious visitation.
3. Acceptable; favored; as, gracious in the sight of the people.
4. Condescending and courteous in manner to inferiors.
5. In Scripture, chiefly of God; as, the Lord is gracious and full of compassion, Psa. 145.
corruption_summary: In common speech gracious has shrunk to good manners — a gracious host, a gracious loser. Scripture's word is a description of God stooping to sinners who deserve the opposite.
corruption_paragraphs: The etiquette sense is not false, only tiny. Courtesy is a real virtue and a faint image of the thing, but when gracious means chiefly well-mannered the sentence the LORD is gracious loses its force, and the doctrine of grace loses its home in ordinary language. The Hebrew chanan keeps the direction of the motion visible: it is a stooping, a superior bending to an inferior, and grace by definition moves downward to those who cannot reciprocate.

Jonah 4:2 supplies the sharper correction. Jonah did not misunderstand God's graciousness; he understood it exactly and hated it, because it was aimed at Nineveh. That exposes a temptation nearer to most of us than the etiquette error: gladness at grace received and resentment at grace extended. Any doctrine of grace a man is willing to preach to himself but unwilling to see applied to his enemy has stopped being the doctrine of Psalm 145:8. The principle to recover is that God's graciousness is his own settled character, not a policy he adopts toward people we approve of.
roots_summary: Hebrew channun is gracious, from chanan, to bend or stoop in kindness; chen is the favour so shown. Greek chrestos is kind or good, and charis is grace itself, the free favour of God.
roots_lines: Hebrew channun (H2587) — gracious; used almost exclusively of God, never as a casual compliment.
Hebrew chanan (H2603) — to bend or stoop in kindness, to show favour to an inferior.
Hebrew chen (H2580) — grace, favour; what Noah found in the eyes of the LORD.
Greek chrestos (G5543) — kind, good, gracious; Peter's word in the Lord is gracious.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace; unmerited favour, the New Testament's central term for God's saving disposition.
usage: Of the standing Old Testament refrain: the LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger (Psalm 103:8).
Of the attribute a resentful prophet fled from: I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful (Jonah 4:2).
Of grace known by experience: if so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious (1 Peter 2:3).
scriptures: Psalm 103:8
The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy.
Psalm 145:8
The LORD is gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy.
Jonah 4:2

And he prayed unto the LORD, and said, I pray thee, O LORD, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil.
1 Peter 2:3
If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.

pos: a. (full of mercy, compassionate; rendering Hebrew rachum, Greek eleemon)
etymology: From the Latin merces, hire or reward, through the Old French merci, pity. Hebrew rachum is from rechem, the womb — mercy in Hebrew is visceral, the compassion of a mother for the child she bore, not a cool decision to overlook a fault.
biblical_def: Merciful describes the disposition to withhold deserved judgment and to relieve misery, and Scripture roots it in God before it requires it of men. The Hebrew word is built on the noun for the womb, so mercy in the Old Testament is never bloodless; it is the yearning of one bound to another. Our Lord makes mercy a beatitude with a promise attached: “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7) — not mercy earned by mercy shown, but mercy shown as the evidence of mercy already received, since the unmerciful servant of the parable proves he never understood his own forgiveness. Luke gives the command its measure: “Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6:36), where the standard is not proportion but imitation. Hebrews shows why the incarnation was necessary for mercy of this kind: Christ was made like unto his brethren “that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 2:17). The mercy of our High Priest is not distant pity but the sympathy of one who has been here. Proverbs adds the practical reflex: “The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh” (Proverbs 11:17).
webster_summary: Full of mercy; disposed to pity and spare. The Hebrew word is built on the womb — mercy is visceral compassion, not detached leniency — and Christ our High Priest is merciful because he was made like his brethren.
webster_full: MERCIFUL, a. [from mercy.] Having or exercising mercy; compassionate; tender; disposed to pity offenders and to forgive their offenses.
2. Unwilling to give pain; not cruel; as, a merciful man is merciful to his beast, Prov. 12.
3. Applied to God, ready to pardon; abundant in goodness and truth.
4. In Scripture, blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy, Matt. 5.
5. Of the High Priest, made like unto his brethren that he might be merciful, Heb. 2.
corruption_summary: Mercy is confused with permissiveness — declining to call sin sin. Biblical mercy presupposes real guilt and real judgment deserved; where nothing is owed, nothing is remitted, and mercy has nothing to do.
corruption_paragraphs: The characteristic modern substitution puts tolerance in mercy's place. Tolerance says the offence was not serious; mercy says the offence was serious and will not be exacted. The two are not neighbours but opposites, and the substitution destroys the thing it means to preserve, because a God who overlooks sin is not merciful, merely indifferent. Hebrews 2:17 will not permit the confusion: the merciful High Priest is merciful in the act of making reconciliation for sins, which cost him everything and cost the sinner nothing.

A second error runs opposite and is common among the doctrinally careful: mercy treated as a soft attribute, tolerated in God but suspected in men, so that severity passes for faithfulness. Luke 6:36 forbids it by setting the Father as the pattern — be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful. The principle to recover is that mercy and justice met at the cross rather than cancelling each other. God did not waive the penalty; he bore it. Mercy that costs the merciful nothing is not the mercy Scripture means.
roots_summary: Hebrew rachum is compassionate, from rechem, the womb; chesed is covenant lovingkindness, mercy bound by promise. Greek eleemon is merciful and oiktirmos denotes tender compassions.
roots_lines: Hebrew rachum (H7349) — compassionate, merciful; used of God in the great self-disclosure at Sinai.
Hebrew rechem (H7358) — the womb; the physical root that gives Hebrew mercy its warmth.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — lovingkindness, covenant mercy; steadfast love owed by promise, not by pity alone.
Greek eleemon (G1655) — merciful; the beatitude word, and the description of Christ in Hebrews 2:17.
Greek oiktirmos (G3628) — compassions, tender mercies; Paul's term for the Father of mercies.
usage: Of mercy shown as evidence of mercy received: blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy (Matthew 5:7).
Of the Father as the measure, not the minimum: be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful (Luke 6:36).
Of the incarnation as the ground of priestly mercy: that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest (Hebrews 2:17).
scriptures: Matthew 5:7
Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
Luke 6:36
Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.
Hebrews 2:17

Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.
Proverbs 11:17
The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh.

pos: a. (full of glory, splendid, honourable; rendering Hebrew addir, Greek endoxos)
etymology: From the Latin gloriosus, from gloria, glory. The Hebrew behind it is usually kabod, weight — glory in Scripture is heaviness, substance, the weight a thing has in reality — so what is glorious is what is weighty, not what is merely bright.
biblical_def: Glorious is the adjective of weight. Behind it stands the Hebrew kabod, which means heaviness before it means splendour, so that God's glory is his sheer reality pressing upon creatures, and a glorious thing is one with substance rather than show. Moses' song asks the question the word exists to answer: “Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?” (Exodus 15:11) — and note where the glory is located, in holiness, not in power alone. The New Testament fastens the word to three things chiefly. To the gospel: Paul was entrusted with “the glorious gospel of the blessed God” (1 Timothy 1:11), so that the message itself carries the weight. To the church: Christ will “present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish” (Ephesians 5:27) — the church is not glorious now in appearance, and the verse is a promise about what the Bridegroom will make of her. And to the resurrection body: he “shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). In each case glory is conferred, future, and holy.
webster_summary: Full of glory; weighty, splendid, honourable. Hebrew kabod means heaviness, so the glorious is the substantial — and Scripture applies the word to the gospel, the church, and the resurrection body.
webster_full: GLORIOUS, a. [L. gloriosus.] Illustrious; of exalted excellence and splendor; resplendent with divine perfections.
2. Noble; excellent; renowned; celebrated; as, a glorious victory.
3. Boastful; self-exulting — an older and now rare use.
4. In Scripture, of God; as, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, Exod. 15.
5. Of the body raised; as, fashioned like unto his glorious body, Phil. 3.
corruption_summary: Glory in modern speech means visibility — fame, spectacle, the glow of attention. Scripture's glory is weight, and the Bible locates it in holiness, in a gospel entrusted to a prisoner, and in a church that does not yet look glorious at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Reduce glory to spectacle and worship follows the reduction. Corporate worship then gets designed for the sensation of grandeur — the swell, the lighting, the emotional lift — and is judged by whether it produced one. Exodus 15:11 will not support the equation: the LORD is glorious in holiness, and the regulative principle follows from that, since what God has commanded carries weight and what men have added carries only impression. A service can be impressive and weightless.

The same reduction distorts how a congregation sees itself. Ephesians 5:27 is future and passive: Christ will present the church to himself glorious, without spot or wrinkle. A church that reads present glory into that verse will chase the appearance of it and grow either boastful or despairing when the appearance fails. The principle to recover is that glory in Scripture is conferred and largely still to come. Our present state is the vile body of Philippians 3:21; the glorious body is his, and ours by promise at the resurrection.
roots_summary: Hebrew kabod is weight, hence honour and glory, from kabed, to be heavy; addir is majestic or mighty. Greek doxa is glory and endoxos the adjective, glorious or held in honour.
roots_lines: Hebrew kabod (H3519) — weight, honour, glory; the substance a thing has, not its brightness.
Hebrew kabed (H3513) — to be heavy, to honour; the same root gives the command to honour father and mother.
Hebrew addir (H117) — majestic, mighty, glorious; used of the LORD in Exodus 15.
Greek doxa (G1391) — glory; in the Septuagint it renders kabod and carries its weight into the New Testament.
Greek endoxos (G1741) — glorious, held in honour; the word behind a glorious church.
usage: Of God glorious specifically in holiness: who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises (Exodus 15:11).
Of the gospel entrusted to Paul: according to the glorious gospel of the blessed God (1 Timothy 1:11).
Of the body at the resurrection: fashioned like unto his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).
scriptures: Exodus 15:11
Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?
1 Timothy 1:11
According to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.
Ephesians 5:27
That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
Philippians 3:21
Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.
